scan.target: UOB IT PMO Kanban board (single-file static site) and its repository tooling

summary.headline: The application's own client-side security is genuinely strong - every interpolation is escaped, inputs are sanitised and re-validated at a single door into state, and a restrictive CSP backs it up - so the residual risk sits almost entirely outside the page: an abusable captcha-less notification endpoint and an unpinned MCP dependency in the developer environment.

findings.title: Notification endpoint is entirely client-side with CAPTCHA disabled - inbox flooding and forged notifications
findings.description: The FormSubmit address and the request body are both fully visible in page source, and the request explicitly turns FormSubmit's own CAPTCHA off. The only throttle is MIN_SUBMIT_INTERVAL_MS (index.html:1239), a variable in the attacker's own browser. Anyone who views source obtains the PMO notification address and can POST arbitrary JSON to the endpoint directly, with no rate limit and no proof of origin. The board itself is unaffected - the exposure is the mailbox on the other side.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker opens the published site and reads FORMSUBMIT_ENDPOINT from source. 2. From curl (or a page they control) they POST the same JSON body in a loop, bypassing the in-page interval entirely. 3. The PMO inbox fills with thousands of '[UOB IT PMO] New task ...' emails, or with a handful of convincing forgeries naming a real assignee and a fabricated critical task - recipients have no way to tell a forged notification from a genuine one, since the email carries no shared secret.
findings.recommendation: Two in-constraint steps. (a) Remove _captcha: "false" and let FormSubmit apply its own anti-abuse check - the AJAX endpoint stays the backend and the page still never navigates, so no hard constraint is broken; the cost is that the first submission from a new browser may require solving a challenge. (b) Use a FormSubmit alias / hashed form ID rather than the raw mailbox in the URL, so the real address is not published. Also state in the CONFIG comment (index.html:1163-1175) that the address it holds becomes public the moment the site is deployed.

findings.title: MCP server runs an unpinned npm package with install prompts suppressed
findings.description: npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest resolves and executes whatever version is on the registry at the moment the session starts, with -y suppressing the install confirmation. There is no version pin and no integrity check, so the developer machine executes freshly downloaded third-party code with the developer's full privileges every time Claude Code loads this project. skills-lock.json records SHA-256 hashes for the three installed skills (skills-lock.json:8, :14, :20) but nothing equivalent covers this dependency. This is a developer-environment risk, not a risk to the published site.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. An attacker compromises the @playwright/mcp publishing account, or lands a malicious transitive dependency, and pushes a new patch release. 2. The next time anyone opens this project in Claude Code, npx silently fetches that release - -y means no prompt. 3. The postinstall script or the server process itself runs as the developer: it can read the repository, SSH keys, ~/.claude credentials and environment variables, and can push to the GitHub remote configured in this repo.
findings.recommendation: Pin to an exact version (e.g. @playwright/mcp@0.0.4x) instead of @latest, and review the changelog before bumping it. Optionally install it as a devDependency with a lockfile so npm's integrity hashes apply. This touches only .mcp.json - the site keeps its no-build, no-npm constraint, which governs index.html, not the developer tooling.

findings.title: Clickjacking cover is advisory only - frame-ancestors is inert in a meta tag and GitHub Pages sends no framing header
findings.evidence: frame-ancestors 'none'">   (runtime stand-in at index.html:2216: framed = window.self !== window.top && window.top.location.origin !== window.location.origin;)
findings.description: The code and its own comment (index.html:22-27) correctly acknowledge that browsers ignore frame-ancestors in a meta tag, and warnIfFramed() at index.html:2207-2219 is offered as the stand-in. But the stand-in only raises a toast inside the framed document - it does not stop rendering - and GitHub Pages does not let you add X-Frame-Options or a real CSP response header. The page is therefore genuinely embeddable by any origin.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker frames the published board and positions the iframe so the toast region (bottom of the viewport) is clipped out of view by the parent's own overflow. 2. They overlay opaque content and align an invisible region over the card delete buttons or the Move menu. 3. A visitor lured to the attacker's page clicks through and mutates the board. Impact is bounded: the board holds no credentials, no session and no persistence, so the worst outcome is destruction of a visitor's own in-memory demo data plus a reputational 'UOB PMO' framing for phishing.
findings.recommendation: Strengthen the existing in-page defence rather than adding a server: when warnIfFramed() detects a cross-origin parent, do more than toast - blank or hide the board and render a single 'open this page directly' link, so a framed instance is not clickable at all. That is a change inside the one script block and breaks no constraint. If the site ever moves off GitHub Pages, add a real Content-Security-Policy response header with frame-ancestors 'none'.
findings.constraint_conflict: A real frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options header requires server configuration, which the static GitHub Pages hosting model does not provide; the in-page hardening above is the in-constraint alternative.

findings.title: Markup characters in task fields are forwarded unescaped to FormSubmit's HTML email template
findings.description: escapeHtml() guards the DOM path, but the outbound path does not use it - and it should not need to, because JSON is the transport. The gap is downstream: _template: "table" asks FormSubmit to render the submitted fields into an HTML email. sanitiseText() and sanitiseMultiline() (index.html:1289-1312) strip control characters, bidi overrides and zero-width joiners, but deliberately do not touch < or >, so a title or description containing markup leaves the page verbatim. Whether that markup renders as live HTML depends entirely on FormSubmit's own escaping, which cannot be verified from this repository - hence 'likely' rather than 'confirmed'. Mail clients block script, so the realistic payload is a link or hidden text, not code execution.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker submits a task whose description is an anchor tag pointing at an attacker-controlled 'approval' page - accepted, since sanitiseMultiline() preserves angle brackets. 2. FormSubmit renders the table email. 3. If it does not escape the field, the PMO recipient receives what looks like an internal task notification containing an actionable phishing link, carrying the credibility of the notification channel.
findings.recommendation: Apply escapeHtml() (or a plain < / > replacement) to the free-text fields on the outbound path in notifyNewTask() before they enter JSON.stringify, so the email renders the literal text the user typed regardless of how FormSubmit templates it. Alternatively drop _template: "table" so the notification is delivered as plain text. Either change is a few lines inside the existing script block.

findings.title: GitHub Pages publishes the entire repository, and the Claude Code tooling directory is not gitignored
findings.description: The upload-pages-artifact step ships the whole checked-out tree, so every tracked file is served publicly at the Pages URL - .claude/commands/github-publish.md is already live there today. .gitignore excludes .claude/skills/ (line 13) but not .claude/agents/, .claude/hooks/ or .claude/settings.json. Those are currently untracked, so nothing sensitive is exposed yet; but a single git add -A would publish the agent definitions, the PowerShell Stop hook, and this very security-scan.json - a vulnerability report served from the site it describes.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. The developer commits everything under .claude/ during a routine push. 2. The workflow deploys the whole tree. 3. An attacker fetches /.claude/agents/security-scan.json from the Pages site and reads a ready-made list of this site's weaknesses, plus the hook script and agent prompts describing the developer's local automation.
findings.recommendation: Add .claude/agents/security-scan.json (or the whole .claude/ directory bar the parts you intend to share) to .gitignore, and narrow the deployment: move the published files into a _site/ directory and set path: _site, or add an explicit exclusion step before upload. The site is still a single self-contained index.html, so neither change introduces a build.

findings.title: 404.html carries none of the security headers index.html declares
findings.evidence: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">   - the head runs from line 3 to line 11 with no Content-Security-Policy and no referrer meta, unlike index.html:29-40
findings.description: The error page is served from the same origin as the board and executes its own inline script (404.html:128), yet it declares no CSP, no referrer policy and no framing intent. The script itself is safe - it assigns window.location.pathname via textContent, which cannot inject - so this is a defence-in-depth inconsistency rather than an exploitable flaw: the second layer index.html relies on is simply absent on its sibling page.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL to reach the 404 page and frames it, or relies on the missing no-referrer policy to have the crafted path leak in the Referer header of a later navigation. With the script using textContent there is no injection to chain, so this is a hardening gap, not a live vector.
findings.recommendation: Copy the CSP and referrer meta tags from index.html:29-40 into the 404.html head, tightening connect-src to 'none' since the error page makes no requests. It is a self-contained single file already, so nothing about the constraint set changes.

findings.title: No user-facing notice that task data is transmitted to a third party
findings.evidence: Demo mode - the board lives in memory only. Refreshing the page resets it to the seeded demo data.
findings.description: The toolbar note tells the user the board stores nothing locally, which is true and is a required constraint. What it does not tell them is that every task they add - including the assignee's name at index.html:1827 and project/category detail - is POSTed to formsubmit.co, a third-party relay outside the organisation. A user reading 'the board lives in memory only' could reasonably conclude nothing leaves the page. In a banking PMO context, names attached to work items are personal data, and the absence of a notice is a PDPA/GDPR transparency gap even for a demo.
findings.attack_scenario: Not an attack - a disclosure and governance gap. A user enters a real colleague's name believing it stays in the browser; it is delivered to and retained by a third-party form relay with no processing agreement in place.
findings.recommendation: Extend the existing ephemeral-note paragraph, or add one line to the Add Task modal footer, saying that submitting a task sends its details by email through an external service. One sentence of static markup; no constraint touched.

findings.title: GitHub Actions are referenced by mutable major-version tags rather than commit SHAs
findings.evidence: uses: actions/checkout@v4   (likewise configure-pages@v5 at :32, upload-pages-artifact@v3 at :39, deploy-pages@v4 at :45)
findings.description: A @v4 tag is a moving pointer the action's owner can repoint at any commit. All four here are GitHub-owned actions, so practical likelihood is low, and the workflow's permissions are already correctly minimised (contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write at lines 10-12), which caps what a compromised action could do. Recorded for completeness against SLSA / CISA supply-chain guidance rather than as a live risk.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who compromised a first-party action repository repoints the v4 tag to a malicious commit; the next push to main runs it with this workflow's token, which can write a Pages deployment but cannot write repository contents.
findings.recommendation: Pin each action to a full commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment, and let Dependabot bump them. Workflow-only change.

findings.title: CSP must allow 'unsafe-inline' for both script and style
findings.evidence: script-src 'unsafe-inline';   (and style-src 'unsafe-inline'; at index.html:32, forced by the inline width attribute at index.html:1620: style="width:' + pct + '%")
findings.description: 'unsafe-inline' removes the CSP's ability to distinguish the page's own script from injected script, so the policy's real value here is its origin restrictions (default-src 'none', connect-src limited to formsubmit.co, form-action 'none', base-uri 'none') rather than script control. For script-src this follows directly from the single-file constraint and is not a defect. For style-src it is driven by one inline width attribute on the health meter, which is avoidable. Recorded so the policy's strength is not overstated: it constrains where injected code could reach, not whether it runs.
findings.attack_scenario: Prerequisite is an XSS that does not currently exist - every interpolation in the render path is escaped. Were one introduced, 'unsafe-inline' would let the injected script execute; the origin restrictions would still block loading remote code and block exfiltration to any host other than formsubmit.co.
findings.recommendation: Optionally drop style-src to a hash, or remove the need for it by rendering the health bar width through a small set of fixed-width utility classes (e.g. 5% steps) instead of an inline style attribute. Leave script-src as it is and keep escapeHtml() discipline as the primary control - the comment block at index.html:8-27 already states this correctly.
findings.constraint_conflict: script-src 'unsafe-inline' cannot be removed without either an external .js file or a hash that must be recomputed on every edit; the single-file, no-build constraint makes the current setting the right trade-off.

strengths: Complete output encoding on every string-built markup path: escapeHtml() (index.html:1272) is applied to every interpolated value in renderCard (index.html:1425-1528), renderBoard (index.html:1533-1560), renderSummary (index.html:1587-1594) and fillSelect (index.html:1845-1851). All nine innerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML writes were traced to their inputs and no unescaped user-controlled interpolation was found - the only bare values are computed integers and percentages.
The two places user text meets the DOM outside the string path use textContent, not innerHTML: the celebration dialog (index.html:1652-1656) and showToast (index.html:1791).

Input normalisation at the trust boundary: CONTROL_CHARS (index.html:1268) strips control characters, zero-width joiners and bidi overrides, closing the display-spoofing gap that escaping alone leaves open - an unusually mature control for an artefact this size.

Defence in depth via a genuinely restrictive CSP: default-src 'none' with connect-src limited to the one endpoint (index.html:30-37) means an injected script could neither load remote code nor exfiltrate the board to another host.

Single-door state mutation with allowlist re-validation: addTask (index.html:1723-1749) re-sanitises free text, re-applies length caps, and re-checks project/category/priority/status against their arrays rather than trusting the form, so a tampered option cannot smuggle a value in.

Third-party request hygiene: credentials: "omit", referrerPolicy: "no-referrer", cache: "no-store" and an AbortController timeout (index.html:1806-1817, NOTIFY_TIMEOUT_MS at index.html:1240) keep cookies and the page URL out of the outbound call and prevent a stalled request from wedging the UI.
Email header injection is prevented as a side effect of sanitiseText(): newlines are stripped before task.title reaches the _subject field at index.html:1819.
Availability guards are explicit and enforced at the only entry point: MAX_TASKS (index.html:1238) bounds memory growth, and the submit interval is checked inside validateForm (index.html:1946-1949).

Drag-and-drop treats the dataTransfer payload as untrusted: the dropped ID is resolved through findTask() and the target status through STATUSES before any mutation (index.html:2065-2067, moveTask at index.html:1752-1755), so an external drag cannot inject a task.
The 404 page's inline script writes location.pathname via textContent (404.html:128) rather than innerHTML - the obvious DOM XSS in a page of that shape is correctly avoided.
Workflow permissions are minimised to exactly what a Pages deployment needs, with concurrency queued rather than cancelled (.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml:10-17).
No eval, no Function constructor, no document.write, no javascript: URL, no inline event-handler attributes and no !important anywhere in index.html - verified by grep across the file.
The one external link uses rel="noopener noreferrer" with target="_blank" (index.html:1690), and its parameters are encodeURIComponent-wrapped.
residual_risk: After the recommended changes the residual risk is low and appropriate for a training artefact. The application layer is already close to the ceiling of what a static, unauthenticated, no-persistence page can achieve: with no credentials, no session, no server-side state and nothing stored between refreshes, the classic web risks - broken access control, injection into a datastore, session fixation, insecure deserialisation - have no substrate to act on. What cannot be eliminated within the constraints is (a) the absence of real security response headers, since GitHub Pages does not serve them, leaving the framing defence in-page and advisory; (b) the fact that any client-side rate limit is enforced in the attacker's own browser, so the notification endpoint's abuse resistance ultimately depends on FormSubmit's controls rather than on this page; and (c) the trust placed in FormSubmit as a third-party processor of task data, which is a governance decision already fixed by the specification. All three are acceptable here because the data is fictional demo content and the artefact is explicitly labelled as not an official system (index.html:1042).
notes: CLAUDE.md hard constraints were treated as design decisions, not findings. Specifically NOT reported: absence of localStorage/sessionStorage/cookies (deliberate, and the toolbar note at index.html:1025 says so); the single-file structure and its consequent inline script and style; the lack of a build step, package manager, framework or dependency lockfile for the site; the absence of any external script, font or image; and FormSubmit as the sole backend. None of the recommendations above require breaking any of these.

The FormSubmit address at index.html:1175 is still the placeholder YOUR_EMAIL@example.com, so no real mailbox is exposed today, and no secret, token or credential was found anywhere in the repository. SEC-001 describes what becomes true the moment a real address is substituted, which README.md:38 instructs the operator to do.

The WhatsApp number at index.html:1187 is likewise an inert placeholder (+65 0000 0000 cannot be allocated), and the widget only builds outbound wa.me links - nothing is sent from the page, as the panel footer states.
The whole of index.html (2241 lines) was read, not sampled. No XSS was found and none is reported: asserting one on a page this consistently escaped would be speculation rather than a finding.

SEC-004 is the only finding whose downstream behaviour could not be verified from the source - FormSubmit's own escaping is outside this repository - and it is marked confidence 'likely' for that reason. Every other finding quotes a line that exists in the tree as scanned.

skills-lock.json was reviewed: it pins three third-party skills by SHA-256 (lines 8, 14, 20), which is the right pattern. It is gitignored (.gitignore:14) and the skill content itself is not in the repository, so it is not part of the published attack surface. It is cited in SEC-002 only as the contrast with the unpinned MCP dependency.

.claude/hooks/task-complete.ps1 and .claude/settings.json were read for completeness. The Stop hook runs powershell.exe with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, but against a fixed in-repo script path with no untrusted input interpolated into the child command, so it is not reported as a finding; it matters to SEC-005 only in that publishing it would disclose local automation.
Out of scope: the PDF course material and the .docx under docs/ (both gitignored), the rendered PNG screenshots, and any assessment of FormSubmit's or GitHub Pages' own infrastructure security.

No dynamic testing was performed - this is a static review. A browser-based pass (drag/drop edge cases, focus restoration under rapid re-render, CSP violation reports) would complement it but was not required to reach the findings above.
